rationale: Both passages tell the same short story in the same order: a man with a hundred sheep loses one, leaves the ninety-nine, goes after the one, finds it, and there is more joy over it than over the ninety-nine; each ends "In the same way" (BSB, Matthew 18:14 and Luke 15:7). In this app's BSB, "hundred sheep" occurs only at 1 Kings 4:23 (a list of provisions), Matthew 18:12 and Luke 15:4, and "ninety-nine" outside these two passages only in Genesis 17:1 and 17:24, of Abraham's age (script searches). That shared narrative sequence is why the type is parallel, following conn-matt11-woes-luke10 and conn-matt5-salt-mark9, where the same saying in two different settings is graded parallel/strong. The differences are large and are reported rather than smoothed. The setting: in Matthew the story is told to disciples about "these little ones" (18:14); in Luke to Pharisees and scribes who complained that Jesus "welcomes sinners" (15:2), and it ends on "one sinner who repents" (15:7). The verbs: Matthew's sheep "goes astray" (planethe, planomenon, 18:12-13), Luke's is "lost" (apolesas, apololos, 15:4); Matthew uses the "perish" root only at the end (apoletai, 18:14). The place: "on the hills" in Matthew, "in the pasture" (Greek "in the wilderness") in Luke. Commentators read on Bible Hub disagree on the history but agree it is the same parable: Meyer, Luke records "the same beautiful parable, though in a different connection"; the Pulpit Commentary, it is found in Luke "with some variations, delivered to a different audience"; Gill, "this parable was twice delivered." Calvin, on 18:12, says Luke's narrative "presents to us a somewhat different object." The label is strong, not explicit, because the setting and application differ and neither Gospel refers to the other.
